playbook:
When asked to hide, pick a cell away from any spots recently guessed successfully against me; if another boat has hit me on cell n recently, avoid n and adjacent cells. Prefer central cells early (4–6) unless pattern or opponent behavior suggests otherwise, but do not repeat the exact same hide more than twice in a row. Rotate unpredictably among a constrained set of 3–4 candidate cells (prefer a central triad plus one flank) rather than a pure random pick each round.

When the standing order directs me to fire at a particular station, target that station as ordered. Choose the fired cell by inferring that station’s probable hide from the public ledger of past hits and misses and from notes:
- If I have a confirmed hit on that target’s cell, I may fire that cell once more immediately (capitalizing on inertia), but if the follow-up returns a miss, abandon that cell and switch to another candidate from my rotation.
- If I have no confirmed hits, favor central/mid-range cells (4–6) as initial probes, but vary within my candidate set to avoid becoming predictable.
- Prefer cells that others have recently hit on that target only if those reports are credible and not clearly being used as deception.
- Do not fire on Harbor; never provoke the payroll jettison penalty.

When the office privately tells me my shot result, file the exact required public claim (must match office). Do not attempt to lie—claims are enforced and my credibility matters for signaling and for others’ inferences.

When posting my station note, use it deliberately to build or withdraw signaling credibility:
- If I intend to propose an escort reciprocity, post an explicit short offer naming the intended partner and be prepared to follow through next round.
- If I will not reciprocate, post a neutral phrasing (“none”, “steady on station”) consistently rather than vacillating, to preserve credibility.
- If I suspect an opponent is targeting me, post a note that obfuscates my intentions (neutral) rather than revealing a hide pattern.
- Use notes sparingly: a clear explicit offer is worth more than ambiguous phrasing for securing mutual escort payoff.

When choosing an escort claim, name a partner only when I have either:
- an explicit reciprocal offer from them, or
- a very strong expectation of reciprocation based on recent mutual behavior.
Otherwise claim none. The mutual-escort payoff (+5 each) is high enough that I prioritize firm signals and follow-through rather than hoping for accidental reciprocation.

When I score hits on another boat, capitalize immediately but not repeatedly:
- Repeat a successful cell once to try to secure damage, but if the next attempt is a miss, assume the target moved or adapted and switch cells.
- Do not fixate on one cell across many rounds; variation prevents being counter-targeted.

When I am hit multiple times by the same opponent, change hiding strategy and note phrasing to break their guess pattern: shift my rotation set and avoid reused cells or obvious central bias. If I suspect deliberate targeting, deprioritize escort offers and play more evasively.

When choosing hide locations across rounds, maintain a balance of unpredictability and limited support for inference:
- Rotate among 3–4 preferred cells, occasionally testing an out-of-set cell only when information suggests an opportunity.
- Avoid adjacent cells to any recent successful shot by opponents against me.

When weighing risking points for escort vs. guarding my own score, prefer escort deals only when the expected mutual payoff is clear (explicit offer or reliable reciprocity). Do not give up escort points for speculative gambles.

When making notes and claims, act to build long-term credibility: truthful public claims, consistent follow-through on any posted escort offers, and predictable adherence to standing orders help extract future mutual-payoff opportunities.

When observing the public ledger of hits/misses and notes, update my model of each opponent’s probable hide and intentions each round and use that model to choose hide and fire cells:
- Track each opponent’s successful hits and misses on others and myself; use their targeting patterns to predict their next hide cells.
- Consider the turn order (Echo->Foxtrot->Gamma) and standing fire sequence when anticipating who will probe whom and when to exploit openings.

Exploit turn/sequence information: because firing order is predictable, anticipate who will be under attack next and tailor my hide and note to either avoid being an easy follow-up target or to cooperate when pursuing mutual escorts.

Never fire on Harbor or respond to provocations that would force payroll jettison—the penalty benefits Harbor and harms me.

Overall tactical posture:
- Preserve and build signaling credibility.
- Use explicit offers and follow-through to secure mutual escort points; otherwise default to none.
- Be adaptive: capitalize on hits but abandon predictable repetition when countered.
- Keep hides unpredictable within a limited set and adjust immediately when opponents demonstrate successful patterns against me.

1.text:
When prompted for a hide, pick a position that balances unpredictability and even coverage: favor center-ish cells early (around 4–6), then randomize within ±2 of center on later rounds. Avoid repeating the same cell two rounds in a row.

If I was hit in a prior round, move from my previous hide to a different cell (do not repeat the same cell two rounds in a row) and bias the move away from where the hit likely came from. After I score a hit, also change hide to reduce predictability and retaliation risk.

When posting a station note, default to a neutral, noncommittal message (e.g., "steady on station"). Do not give positional hints. Use notes only to try to bait or coordinate a reciprocal escort when I have a reasonable basis to expect reciprocation; otherwise remain neutral.

Follow the standing order for targets unless the standing order targets Harbor or there is a clear tactical reason to deviate. Harbor carries payroll; do not fire on Harbor unless I have a deliberate plan to accept being jettisoned and the expected payoff exceeds that cost.

When choosing a fire cell, avoid overly predictable fixed numbers; prefer a probabilistic pattern centered on the middle (around 4–6) but with variance so I do not become easy to track. If I have information (recent hit location, opponent patterns), bias shots to exploit that. If I know a target was hit previously, avoid repeatedly firing the same coordinate immediately.

When the office privately tells me my shot result, report that exact result publicly. The public claim must match the private result; do not attempt deception here.

When naming an escort (salvage), name another boat only if I have good reason to expect reciprocal naming (prior mutual behavior, clear incentive, or explicit signals). If no evidence of reciprocation, claim none to avoid wasting the mutual-bonus opportunity.

If I believe another boat is preparing a reciprocal escort (consistent past mutual claims or explicit coordination), propose mutual escort by naming them. Prefer naming boats that have shown willingness to reciprocate or that benefit from the bonus to induce cooperation.

When deciding to be aggressive (aiming to score hits), weigh the 4 points for a hit against the 1-point penalty to the target and the risk of retaliation and of making my hide predictable. After scoring a hit, change hiding pattern and consider avoiding the same firing cells for a round or two.

When the game enforces conventions or office constraints (validated coordinates, claims must match private info), comply; exploit allowed flex where it improves expected score but do not attempt forbidden mismatches.

Do not rely on consistent deceptive public notes to mask my hide; public notes are low-cost signals and easy to ignore—use them sparingly for coordination rather than camouflage.

Maintain minimal bookkeeping each round: my last hide, whether I was hit, what I hit, and which boats have shown willingness to escort. Use that to decide hide moves, firing bias, and whether to propose salvage.

If points are low late in the patrol and reciprocation seems unlikely, prioritize survival (avoid firing Harbor, avoid becoming an easy target) and small consistent gains (truthful claims, conservative hides). If I am ahead and can pressure others, be willing to take calculated aggressive shots and attempt to provoke costly errors by opponents.

2.text:
When asked to hide, choose a central cell (4–6) in early rounds to reduce predictability; if I remain unhit and opponents have likely deduced a center habit, shift to an off‑center cell (1–3 or 7–9) in later rounds. If I have been hit or see patterns suggesting opponents expect my center choice, pick a less obvious cell immediately.

When an opponent has hit me previously, avoid cells they have used successfully against me and avoid obvious repeat numbers; pick from a different region of the board to reduce the chance of a repeat hit.

When posting a station note, mirror the prevailing neutral tone ("steady on station") by default to avoid drawing attention or revealing intent. Only deviate from neutral notes when I want to deliberately bait or signal and can accept the attendant risk of attracting fire.

Follow standing firing orders for target selection unless there is a clear, high‑value tactical reason to deviate (for example: a safe, high‑probability opportunity to jettison Harbor that outweighs the explicit threat). Do not make attacking Harbor routine; only fire on Harbor if the point transfer and game context justify accepting Harbor's warning and likely retaliation.

When choosing a firing cell, randomize within a constrained set rather than repeating a single number every round. Bias my choices by:
- avoiding cells opponents have recently used successfully against targets,
- avoiding my own recently used fired cells that would make me predictable to the next shooter,
- occasionally selecting a cell that opponents might expect to catch them off guard.

When the office privately tells me the true result of my shot, always file the required public claim that matches the private result (truthful claims are mandatory and preserve credibility).

When my shot hits a target, recognize that the next shooter in sequence may shift their targeting; consider changing my hide or firing randomness after a hit to avoid becoming a predictable retaliation target. If hitting yields strategic advantage (reducing a rival's score), I may accept the increased attention but still vary hides/fires.

When deciding whether to name an escort (salvage claim), name another boat only when I reasonably expect a reciprocal claim (mutual naming yields 5 points each). If reciprocity is unlikely or the escort claim would signal an alliance that can be exploited by others, claim none.

Keep station notes non‑informative about my hidden cell or intended shots; do not reveal weakness or tactical patterns in notes.

If I detect two other boats coordinating (mutual escorts or synchronized hits/notes), exploit openings by increasing my hide and fire randomness and avoid predictable behaviors that make me an easy collateral target.

If my prior pattern has led to being targeted (predictable hides, repeated fired cells, or conspicuous notes), stop repeating that pattern immediately and shift both hide and firing randomness.

Maintain truthful public claims even if lying might appear advantageous; the game enforces claim matching private feedback, so truthfulness is required and preserves reputation for potential reciprocal escort arrangements.

Overall priority order when deciding actions:
1. Preserve my points and avoid becoming an easy retaliation target (adjust hides/fires to reduce predictability).
2. Follow standing orders for target selection unless a deviation has clear, high value.
3. Use escort claims only when mutual gain is likely.
4. Avoid attacking Harbor except for compelling, calculated opportunities.
5. Keep notes neutral and non revealing.
